title: The Children and the Good Player Award
text:
In the early 1970s, Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett watched children at a nursery school on the Stanford campus during free play and noted which ones already liked to draw with a new set of colored markers. Those children were then invited, one at a time, to draw for the researchers.

Some were told in advance that if they drew, they would receive a "Good Player" certificate with a gold seal and a ribbon. Others drew without any mention of a reward and then got the same certificate as a surprise. A third group neither expected nor received anything.

About two weeks later, the markers were put out again during ordinary free play, with no adults asking anyone to draw, and observers recorded how much time each child spent with them. Children who had drawn in order to earn the certificate now drew much less than before, about half as much as the other two groups. The children who had received the surprise reward, or none at all, kept drawing as they had before.

The researchers called this the overjustification effect: when an expected reward is attached to something a child already enjoys, the child may start to see it as work done for a prize.
lesson: Be careful about paying children, or anyone, for what they already love doing. Unexpected appreciation is safer than a promised prize.
people: Mark Lepper, David Greene, Richard Nisbett
location: Bing Nursery School, Stanford University, Stanford, USA
source: Lepper, M. R., Greene, D., and Nisbett, R. E. (1973). Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the 'overjustification' hypothesis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 28(1), 129-137.
